Mapping Medicine's Future

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As the UK continues an ambitious project to map the genomes of 100 thousand people with cancer and rare diseases, we discover that Africa is planning to follow suit.

Unique Selling Point:
While genetic medicine is in its relative infancy in South Africa, Carte Blanche will gain insight into its potential to shape future medicine by visiting the acclaimed 100 000 Genomes Project run bu the NHS in the U.K. This will provide our viewers with a practical guide on the ambitions of our own medical research council as it captures the unique genetic "fingerprints" of a broad section of the population and uses that information to refine what is becoming known as "precision medicine".

Summary:
The 100 000 Genomes Project in the UK aims to capture - through an incredibly complex but increasingly practical process - the information contained in the genes of people with rare diseases and cancers. That involves sequencing the 3 billion letters of each persons genome, and examining where the likely "genetic malfunction" that led to a particular disease is taking place. Once that information is collated and cross-checked - and the complexities of how that data is stored and protected overcome - it'll be far easier to detect and therefore treat those diseases in other people.

This is the future of medicine: Targeted diagnosis and treatment at a genetic level based on information about your unique "biological architecture" which will be deciphered and eventually stored on a massive data base.

It's a process already underway in many parts of the world, and one being grappled with by our own Medical Research Council. In spite of the enormous logistical and resource challenges, there's a plan to do in Africa what is being done in the UK.

Press Release:


Genetically Mapping Medicine’s Future
It’s the future of medicine – using genetic mapping to enable precise and personalised treatment for patients. Researchers in Britain are working on this ambitious project which aims to map the genomes of thousands of participants with cancer and rare diseases and create a new genomic medicine service. Now a team of local specialists from the continent are working hard to ensure Africa isn’t left behind. Carte Blanche tracks this new development in medicine.
Producer: John Webb
Presenter: John Webb


Script:


Gene Mapping Script.

VO: Just a few months ago, a Chinese researcher made a shock announcement:

VO: Using almost alien-like technology, he claimed to have successfully edited the genes of unborn twins to make their cells resistant to HIV. It was an experiment condemned by the scientific community as irresponsible at best, downright dangerous at worst – not least because it opened the door to custom-made kids – engineering at its most frightening.

ITV: Jantina De Vries [04:33] With just one person going ahead and doing it. He's made alterations to our common human genetic heritage in some way.

VO: Jantina De Vries is an Associate Professor at the University of Cape Town. She’s also one of two South Africans on a high-level panel grappling with the ethics of gene-editing.

ITV: Jantina De Vries STRAP: “Assoc. Prof: Health Sciences, UCT” [08:46] the biggest concern there is that people who have access to resources would start to use these technologies for enhancements and that that will be unfair. That if you could design your babies to outperform everybody else in sports or in cognition, in educational performance, that that would be inappropriate.

VO: Clearly, there’s a need for global standards, a kind of international rule book that makes clear where a line should be drawn.

ITV: Jantina De Vries [10:31] there's kind of a consensus that if it's beneficial to health and if it helps people become healthy, then we should use technologies. There's also equal consensus that if, if things are used to improve something that is already fully functional, then maybe we should be more cautious.

VO: The ethical dilemmas aside, the benefits of research at this level of the human body are revolutionary. It began when more than two decades of international collaboration unlocked the sequence of the human Genome, unravelling the pattern of billions of chemical bases contained in our DNA – basically, our body’s instruction manual. It’s a seemingly endless pattern of four letters – A-T-G and C - which reveal that humans are remarkably similar but quite different too.

Link: This is my cameraman – to the best of our best knowledge we’re unrelated. Now, scientists estimate that our Genomes are around 99.9% the same. That probably seems like not much difference at all but – if you crunch the numbers – it means there are about three million differences across the entire Genome.

VO: That figure- which in time is likely to get bigger - explains things like Toby’s ginger hair and my premature greyness, but it holds more sinister information too. Like that contained in the 0.1% of this man:

VO: … an apparently healthy individual having a workout. Appearances, though, can be deceptive. This is Gragevis Bakatukanda and he has an incurable genetic disease. He arrived in South Africa from the DRC more than a decade ago with a misdiagnosis and in fits of pain.

ITV: Gragevis Bakatukanda STRAP “Sickle Cell Patient” [01:17] And then when I got here, even on the way here, I was terribly sick. So after that they diagnosed that I had sickle cell.

VO: Sickle Cell Disease is inherited from the parents and affects millions around the globe. In the developing world, where the disease is most common, up to 90 percent of children born with it die before the age of five. Bakatukanda defied those odds but still deals with episodes of excruciating pain.

ITV: Gragevis Bakatukanda [04:53] It's extremely painful. Like sometimes if when I used to have back pains I had to find a specific position to sit comfortable one and if I just try to turn or move it starts paining even worse CUT and normally I only require some morphine just to ease the pain up.

VO: Our red blood cells – which transport oxygen throughout the body – are shaped like a disc. But, in people with Sickle Cell Disease, they become rigid and shaped like a banana or sickle. As a result, they often stick to each other and get jammed in the blood vessels.

VO: Bakatukanda is part of a generation on the cusp of a medical revolution but not quite able to fully benefit from it. Something true of people with a range of diseases.

ITV Rizwana Mia [00:01:58] they say that 50 percent of modern-day drugs commonly used drugs are not effective in their target populations. So, this is where the work starts. And this is why this is so important for everybody.

VO: Rizwana Mia is from the Medical Research Council, and she has a vision of the future in which medicine is personalized and more precise.

ITV Rizwana Mia STRAP “Programme Manager: SAMRC Genomics Centre” [00:21:15] Imagine if you could take a pinprick of blood and be able to understand just where you are at every day in terms of your own health. You know small things and just be able to keep a check on it and be able to take the correct enzymes because you're lacking it or have a doctor create a targeted based treatment for you like in an hour. That's sort of the utopia that everybody wants to have.

Link: It’s a Utopia that countries like the United Kingdom appear to be accelerating towards with massive projects already sequencing the Genomes of thousands and thousands of people.

VO: A pioneering initiative by the UK government has sequenced the Genomes - the hugely complex personal DNA codes – of tens of thousands of people with rare diseases and certain cancers. Called the 100 Thousand Genomes Project, it is stunningly ambitious. It provides a truly massive data base collected from the DNA of its participants which can be used as a kind of reference library. New cell samples will be compared to the information already collected, meaning faster diagnoses and – most importantly – more precise treatment. You can even imagine the impact on complex diseases like cancer where, instead of a one-size-fits-all approach, patients are given more personal and effective treatments. It’s the gold-standard our own Medical Research Council is aspiring to and one the rest of Africa needs to emulate.

ITV: Rizwana Mia [00:32] we in South Africa will look at it from a different perspective because we have different issues (CUT) will we will try and position ourselves to create an African genome study and do some work around unpacking our genetic diversity.

ITV Ambroise Wonkam [09:10] we have the oldest population of humankind, so we have 10 times more variation than the youngest population from Europe or from Asia for example.

VO: Professor Ambroise Wonkam, is director of the Genetic Medicine of African Populations research centre, or GeneMAP, at UCT.

ITV Ambroise Wonkam STRAP “Director: GeneMAP, UCT” [09:10] Every single geneticist in the world, whether you're in Europe, or in America, at some point you would need to compare a variation to African genome variation. But, unfortunately, up to now the representativity of African genome in the database that are publicly available is very low.

VO: Africa, he says, is in need of significant investment in genomics research.

ITV: Ambroise Wonkam [20:15] here we are talking about human right. It means (CUT) that some of those many, many patients that we know have extremely rare disease will not have access to treatment. It is already in the case now. So that means that we need to accelerate the path of genomic medicine.

ITV Jack Morrice [01:41:640] 95 percent of the people of the human genome tested come from people of white European descent which means that sickle cell disease has largely been understudied and underdeveloped.

VO: Jack Morrice, part of the GeneMAP team focussing on Sickle Cell, is another advocate of more inclusive Genome sequencing. In the meantime, he’s trying to fill in the gaps – which is easier said than done.

ITV: Jack Morrice STRAP “Post-Doctoral Researcher, UCT” [00:04:04.120] We know that there is a mutation in and we know exactly where in the genome it occurs which gives rise to this disease. But I think what we're learning is that, well, as geneticists we're learning that genetic disease is much more complicated than that.

VO: Scientists are now discovering that that gene doesn’t act alone but is influenced by other unknown parts of the Genome. It means Morrice and his colleagues have to cast their net wider in their quest for answers – something they’re doing with data from Sickle Cell patients in places like Cameroon, Ghana and Nigeria.

ITV: Jack Morrice[00:04:59.290] we are trying to sequence the entire genome to try and (CUT) look for patterns in the genome that go beyond this single cell mutation that might help us to better understand the disease.

VO: Bakatukanda might not fully benefit from that better understanding. But, in time, current medicines will be tailored, and new therapies developed. And the thing about science, is that developments in one area often lead to developments in others.

ITV: Jantina De Vries [18:08] It's fascinating. And what is happening in the, not just in the, in the genetics sphere, but also in the technological sphere like the developments in AI, the developments in robotics, um, discussions about possible moves towards transhumanism and what that means for how we structure our societies. It's, it's fascinating and South Africans are contributing.

ENDS.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: While genetic medicine is in its relative infancy in South Africa, Carte Blanche will gain insight into its potential to shape future medicine by visiting the acclaimed 100 000 Genomes Project run bu the NHS in the U.K. This will provide our viewers with a practical guide on the ambitions of our own medical research council as it captures the unique genetic "fingerprints" of a broad section of the population and uses that information to refine what is becoming known as "precision medicine".
metadata.Summary: The 100 000 Genomes Project in the UK aims to capture - through an incredibly complex but increasingly practical process - the information contained in the genes of people with rare diseases and cancers. That involves sequencing the 3 billion letters of each persons genome, and examining where the likely "genetic malfunction" that led to a particular disease is taking place. Once that information is collated and cross-checked - and the complexities of how that data is stored and protected overcome - it'll be far easier to detect and therefore treat those diseases in other people. This is the future of medicine: Targeted diagnosis and treatment at a genetic level based on information about your unique "biological architecture" which will be deciphered and eventually stored on a massive data base. It's a process already underway in many parts of the world, and one being grappled with by our own Medical Research Council. In spite of the enormous logistical and resource challenges, there's a plan to do in Africa what is being done in the UK.
